title: SLO Steward Transfer & Capacity Reconciliation Docket
author: Ayesha Khan
content:
Summary

This docket prescribes a standard, auditable procedure for (a) transferring SLO stewardship when services, models, or ownership move between teams, and (b) reconciling capacity allocations against live SLO consumption. The document ties together SLO definitions, error-budget accounting, capacity calculations, runbook alignment, telemetry verification, and post-handoff acceptance criteria. Use this page when owners change, when a service changes behavior (new model, new batching pattern), or after capacity audits.

Scope

- Services and model-serving endpoints hosted on Redwood inference runtime (hosted, dedicated, private).
- Multi-tenant and single-tenant model endpoints, embedding and generation workloads.
- Includes warm-pools, quantized variants, and fallback routing policies.

Why this matters

Misaligned stewardship and stale capacity assumptions cause silent SLO drift, surprise error-budget exhaustion, or unnecessary cost due to over-provisioning. A reproducible handoff process reduces operational surprises and shortens incident MTTR.

Definitions (quick)

- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., p99 latency <= 250ms).
- SLI: Service Level Indicator (measured metric feeding the SLO).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO over a chosen window (daily/weekly/rolling 28d).
- Capacity reservation: committed GPU/replica headroom assigned to a tenant or model class.

Owner and roles

- Outgoing steward: current SLO owner responsible for producing handoff artifacts.
- Incoming steward: new owner taking responsibility for SLOs and runbooks.
- SRE reviewer: on-call SRE who validates telemetry, dashboards and capacity reconciliation.
- Platform ops: team that executes capacity changes for Dedicated/Private deployments.

Prerequisites before transfer (outgoing steward tasks)

1) SLO doc and canonical SLI(s): list of SLOs, measurement windows, and alert thresholds.
2) Error-budget ledger export: last 90 days of SLI values, burn-rate history, and any throttling actions taken.
3) Capacity profile: historical p50/p90/p99 latency vs qps, GPU memory usage, model warm-pool hit ratio, and cold-start counts.
4) Dashboards and alerts: links to dashboards, exact PromQL/Flux queries, and alert runbooks.
5) Deployment manifest and autoscale policy: replicas, limits/requests, GPU SKU, batch sizes, and autoscaler configuration.
6) Known caveats: quantization regressions, model warmup windows, traffic seasonality, tenant priority lanes.

Handoff checklist (atomic acceptance items; incoming steward must tick each):

1) Verify metadata: service name, route(s), owner contact info, SLA contractual obligations.
2) Verify SLI replay: run replay on the canonical 28-day window and compare numbers to ledger. Accept if discrepancy <= 2%.
3) Validate alert firing: trigger test alert (non-disruptive) or simulate via synthetic load to confirm alert-to-chat flow and PagerDuty routing.
4) Confirm capacity matrix: confirm committed tokens/replicas and identify if additional headroom is required.
4a) If capacity shortfall > 15% on p99 under projected traffic, open a capacity request (see Capacity Request template below).
5) Ensure runbook ownership: incoming steward signs off on runbook steps and escalation chain.
6) Post-handoff probation: a 14-day observability window where the incoming steward retains right-of-first-response.

Capacity reconciliation procedure (quantitative)

Step 1 — Collate metrics (last 28d, hourly granularity):
- R(t): requests per hour (or token rate).
- Lp99(t): observed p99 latency.
- GPU_util(t): GPU utilization per replica.
- Warm_hit_ratio(t): fraction of requests served from warm pool.

Step 2 — Headroom model (example formula)
- Baseline replicas required = ceil( mean(R)/capacity_per_replica )
- Target replicas for p99 SLO = ceil( baseline_replicas * (1 + safety_factor) )
- safety_factor default = max(0.15, peak_95th_percentile(R)/mean(R) - 1)

Notes: capacity_per_replica must be empirically derived for the model variant under expected sequence-length distribution. See Appendix A for experimental run procedure.

Step 3 — Error-budget to capacity translation (heuristic)
- If current burn rate > 2x sustained over 3 hours and error-budget remaining < 25%: consider immediate mitigation (scale out, enable fallback model, reduce max tokens).
- If bursty traffic exceeds capacity but burn-rate remains within budget: prefer throttling non-critical tenants before scaling.

Capacity Request template (for Platform Ops)

- Requested by: [incoming steward name]
- Service: [service route / model id]
- Current committed: [replicas / GPU type]
- Observed headroom shortfall: [x%] with supporting metrics (link to slice)
- Proposed change: [add n replicas / upgrade GPU SKU to X / reserve burst pool Y]
- Validation plan: how will we verify SLO improvement post-change
- Rollback plan: what to revert and timeline

Incident / SLO-breach play (quick checklist)

1) Triage: acknowledge alert and annotate burn-rate/remaining budget.
2) Short-term mitigations (pick at most two to limit blast radius):
   - Enable model variant fallback (quantized fallback)
   - Temporarily reduce max tokens per request by 20%
   - Add temporary replicas (Platform Ops) with 10–15 minute warmup plan
   - Throttle low-priority API keys using token-priority gating
3) Communication: update status page, route to customer-success for impacted tenants, and escalate to engineering manager if breach > 2 hours.
4) Stabilize: verify SLI trend recovering for two consecutive p99 windows (1h each).
5) Post-incident: open incident review and follow Incident Review Standards below.

Incident Review Standards (evidence required)

- Timeline: exact event timeline with UTC timestamps.
- Telemetry artifacts: raw SLI samples, burn-rate graphs, CPU/GPU telemetry correlated to incident, and sampling of tokens/requests for affected timeframe.
- Runbook actions: record what mitigations run and why (who executed).
- Customer impact: list tenants affected and downstream observability (error rates, latencies).
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence mapping: show how the hypothesis accounts for all artifacts.
- Action items: prioritized remediation with owners and target dates.
- Follow-up verification plan: specific metrics and thresholds that show completion.

Tooling integration (practical snippets)

PromQL examples (alerts)
- SLI p99 latency (example):
  - 'histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le, job))'
- Error budget burn-rate:
  - 'sum(increase(slo_violations_total[1h])) / sum(increase(requests_total[1h]))'
\nLogs / traces
- Correlate trace_id across request path: use the request header x-rw-trace and join traces with tokens emitted.
\nSQL for ledger export (example)
- SELECT bucket_start, count(*) AS requests, quantile_cont(0.99) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms) AS p99_ms FROM slo_samples WHERE service='svc-x' AND bucket_start >= now() - interval '28 days' GROUP BY bucket_start ORDER BY bucket_start;
\nRunbook snippets (ops commands)
- Scale replicas (for Dedicated):
  - 'platformctl capacity scale --service svc-x --replicas N --gpu a100-80gb --reason "SLO reconciliation"'
- Flush warm pool cache (non-disruptive):
  - 'rwctl model warm-pool flush --model-id mdl-123 --region us-west1'
- Apply throttles:
  - 'rwctl throttle set --service svc-x --policy low-priority --rate 50rps'
\nRollout gating and acceptance criteria (post-handoff probation)

- Dashboard parity: incoming steward must have writable copies of live dashboards and maintain identical queries.
- Replay parity: SLI replay discrepancy <= 2% over the canonical 28-day window.
- Alert parity: each alert that impacts SLOs has a documented owning individual and an escalation chain.
- Capacity parity: platform reservations match the reconciled capacity table within +/- 10% or a signed capacity request is pending.

Appendix A — Empirical capacity experiment (short)

1) Prepare a synthetic load harness that mirrors real request distribution (sequence length histogram, user prompt mix, embedding vs generation ratio).
2) Run single-replica saturation test to derive capacity_per_replica for p50, p90 and p99 targets.
3) Repeat with quantized model variant and warm-pool enabled; record delta.
4) Document config (gpu type, batch-size, concurrency) and attach CSV to the handoff packet.

Appendix B — Frequently asked decisions

Q: When should we prefer throttling over scaling?
A: Prefer throttling for short bursts where error-budget is healthy and when scaling would take >20 minutes to materially affect p99.

Q: How long should warm pools be retained for low-traffic tenants?
A: Default 24 hours for dedicated tenants, 6 hours for shared tenants. Adjust based on cold-start cost analysis.

Ownership sign-off

- Outgoing steward: ___________________  Date: __________
- Incoming steward: ___________________  Date: __________
- SRE reviewer: _______________________  Date: __________

This docket is intended to be a canonical, repeatable artifact that both reduces friction during ownership changes and ensures capacity commitments are reconciled with actual SLO needs. If you find gaps, update this page and ping #sre-docs for review.
